801 Solving Trigonometric Equations using the ASTC Method

examples.question_text: Simplify (a) $6\sin\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ and (b) $8\cot\theta\tan\theta$. State the excluded angles in degrees.
examples.solution_text:
(a) $\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}6\sin\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta\\&=6\sin\theta\times\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\\&=6\end{aligned}$

Exclude $\theta=180^\circ k$, where $k\in\mathbb Z$.

(b) $\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}8\cot\theta\tan\theta\\&=8\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\\&=8\end{aligned}$

Both sine and cosine must be non-zero. Exclude $\theta=90^\circ k$, where $k\in\mathbb Z$. On this common domain, $\cot\theta=\frac{1}{\tan\theta}$.

examples.question_text: Simplify (a) $\frac{6}{\sec^2 x}$ and (b) $\frac{9\sin x}{\operatorname{cosec}x}$ for all permissible values of $x$.
examples.solution_text:
(a) $\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{6}{\sec^2 x}\\&=6\left(\frac{1}{\sec x}\right)^2\\&=6\cos^2 x\end{aligned}$

The original expression requires $\cos x\ne0$.

(b) $\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{9\sin x}{\operatorname{cosec}x}\\&=9\sin x\times\sin x\\&=9\sin^2 x\end{aligned}$

The original expression requires $\sin x\ne0$.

examples.question_text: Prove the following identities on their common domains: (a) $6\cos\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta=6\cot\theta$, (b) $7\sin\theta\cot\theta\sec\theta=7$, and (c) $\frac{2\sec\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta}=2\tan\theta$.
examples.solution_text:
(a) $\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=6\cos\theta\operatorname{cosec}\theta\\&=6\cos\theta\times\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\\&=6\cot\theta\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$

This requires $\sin\theta\ne0$.

(b) $\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=7\sin\theta\cot\theta\sec\theta\\&=7\sin\theta\times\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\\&=7\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$

This requires $\sin\theta\ne0$ and $\cos\theta\ne0$.

(c) $\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\frac{2\sec\theta}{\operatorname{cosec}\theta}\\&=\frac{2}{\cos\theta}\times\sin\theta\\&=2\tan\theta\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$

This requires $\sin\theta\ne0$ and $\cos\theta\ne0$.

examples.question_text: Show that $\frac{3(\tan x+1)}{\sec x}-\frac{3(\cot x+1)}{\operatorname{cosec}x}$ is independent of $x$ for all permissible values of $x$.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\frac{3(\tan x+1)}{\sec x}-\frac{3(\cot x+1)}{\operatorname{cosec}x}\\&=3\left(\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}+1\right)\cos x-3\left(\frac{\cos x}{\sin x}+1\right)\sin x\\&=3(\sin x+\cos x)-3(\cos x+\sin x)\\&=0\end{aligned}$

The result is constant, so it is independent of $x$. The original expression requires $\sin x\ne0$ and $\cos x\ne0$.

examples.question_text: Prove that $\frac{9}{9+\sin^2 x}+\frac{1}{1+9\operatorname{cosec}^2 x}=1$ for $\sin x\ne0$.
examples.solution_text: $\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\frac{9}{9+\sin^2 x}+\frac{1}{1+9\operatorname{cosec}^2 x}\\&=\frac{9}{9+\sin^2 x}+\frac{1}{1+\frac{9}{\sin^2 x}}\\&=\frac{9}{9+\sin^2 x}+\frac{\sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x+9}\\&=\frac{9+\sin^2 x}{9+\sin^2 x}\\&=1\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: 6 sinθ cosecθ = 6 on sinθ ≠ 0, excluding θ = 180°k. Also, 8 cotθ tanθ = 8 on sinθ cosθ ≠ 0, excluding θ = 90°k. The reciprocal-tangent identity is correctly limited to this common domain.
1/sec²x = cos²x gives 6 cos²x, retaining cosx ≠ 0. Dividing 9 sinx by cosecx multiplies it by sinx, giving 9 sin²x, retaining sinx ≠ 0.
6 tanα/secα = 6(sinα/cosα)cosα = 6 sinα. Also, 7 secα − 7/cosα = 0. Both calculations hold under the stated restriction cosα ≠ 0.

Manipulating each LHS separately gives 6 cosθ/sinθ = 6 cotθ; 7 sinθ(cosθ/sinθ)(1/cosθ) = 7; and (2/cosθ)sinθ = 2 tanθ. Part (a) requires sinθ ≠ 0; parts (b) and (c) require both sine and cosine non-zero.
Writing s = sinθ and c = cosθ, the expression becomes [5(s+c)/(sc)]/[ (s+c)/s ] = 5/c = 5 secθ. The original domain requires s ≠ 0, c ≠ 0 and s+c ≠ 0; all three restrictions are correctly retained.
The first term becomes 3(sinx+cosx), and the second becomes 3(cosx+sinx). Their difference is 0, independent of x. The original expression requires sinx ≠ 0 and cosx ≠ 0.
For u = sin²x > 0, 1/(1+9 cosec²x) = 1/(1+9/u) = u/(u+9). Thus the LHS is 9/(9+u)+u/(9+u) = 1, matching the RHS without operating on both sides.
